title: AWS CWI Training in Oklahoma City, OK: 6-Day Exam Prep
description: Six-day AWS CWI exam prep for Oklahoma City pipeline, oilfield, Tinker aerospace and structural welders: corporate, online or one-to-one.
h1: AWS CWI Exam Prep in Oklahoma City: Six Days for Oil and Gas, Aerospace and Construction Welding Inspectors
html:
Oklahoma City welders build and repair a wide mix of steel: flowlines, gathering systems and compressor stations in the surrounding oil and gas fields, aircraft and engine work at Tinker Air Force Base, and the structural frame of a downtown that is putting up a new arena. When an owner, a contract or a QC manager wants proof that the person accepting those welds knows the code, the credential named is usually the AWS Certified Welding Inspector (CWI). Atlantis NDT prepares candidates for that examination with a six-day (6-day) course covering all three parts: Part A Fundamentals, Part B Practical and Part C Code Application. Oklahoma candidates can take it as corporate delivery at their employer's facility, as online study at their own pace, or as six days of one-to-one sessions with the instructor. AWS administers the examination, decides eligibility and issues the certification; Atlantis certifies nobody. There is no Atlantis classroom in Oklahoma City. The company works from two offices, in Houston, Texas and Hyderabad, India, and reaches central Oklahoma through the three formats below. For a quote, send an Oklahoma City CWI enquiry.

How the six days reach an Oklahoma City candidate

Every format follows one outline. Two days build the fundamentals: welding processes, AWS terms, joint design, welding symbols, metallurgy, destructive and nondestructive testing, safety and the inspector's duties. One day rehearses the practical, one day is spent inside the code book you will choose for Part C, one day is timed practice papers, and the last day goes to weak areas and exam logistics. The day-by-day plan is on the AWS CWI exam prep course page. What changes between formats is who takes part and how the time is spread.

Corporate: a company preparing a group

An oilfield service company, pipeline contractor, structural fabricator or aerospace supplier in the metro can have the six days delivered on its own premises. The practical day uses the company's fillet gauges, bridge cam gauges and real welds from its yard or shop, and the code day follows the books the group will choose, so the practice looks like the work those people accept every week.

Online: an individual studying alone

Individuals receive a study plan built on the six-day outline, course materials, original practice questions and timed practice papers, and an instructor answers questions as they work. There are no scheduled class times. That suits a field hand on a rotation in western Oklahoma as well as someone working rotating shifts at the depot.

One-to-one: six days with the instructor

A single candidate can book six days of one-to-one sessions with the instructor, held online or in person at a place agreed when booking. It fits a QC lead whose employer needs one person ready for a contract, or a welder who passed two parts and wants every hour spent on the third.

In every format the practice questions are original, written by Atlantis to the subject areas AWS publishes. They do not come from any AWS examination, and AWS has not approved, accredited or endorsed the course.

What gets welded around Oklahoma City

Oil and gas in the surrounding fields

Oklahoma City has long been an oil and gas head-office town, although in early 2026 both Devon Energy and Expand Energy, the company formed when Chesapeake Energy and Southwestern Energy merged, announced moves of their headquarters to Houston. The welding was never in the office towers anyway; it happens out in the field: well-pad piping, flowlines, gathering systems, compressor stations, gas processing plants and the separators and tanks between them. Federal pipeline safety rules in 49 CFR Parts 192 and 195 incorporate API 1104 for pipeline welding, and the Oklahoma Corporation Commission oversees pipeline safety on many lines that stay inside the state. Inside plants and stations, procedures are qualified under ASME Section IX and the piping follows B31.3 or B31.8. A CWI who can read a procedure qualification record, check a welder's qualified ranges and accept a girth weld visually is useful at every stage of that chain.

Tinker Air Force Base and aerospace repair

The Oklahoma City Air Logistics Complex at Tinker is one of the Air Force's major depots. Its fact sheet describes a workforce of more than 9,000 military and civilian professionals doing programmed depot maintenance and modification on the KC-46, KC-135, B-1B, B-52, E-3 and the Navy's E-6, and overhauling engines that include the F100, F101, F108, F110, F117, F118, F119 and TF33. Separate groups handle aircraft, commodities, propulsion and maintenance support. Depot repairs follow Air Force technical orders and engineering instructions rather than a civilian construction code, so the CWI is not the entry ticket to depot jobs. The skills the examination tests still carry over: accurate weld measurement, reading a procedure against its qualification record, and finding an acceptance limit quickly. For contractors and suppliers doing aerospace fusion welding, AWS D17.1 is the Part C book closest to their work.

A downtown building cycle

The city is building Continental Coliseum, the new downtown home of the Thunder, with the Flintco and Mortenson joint venture coordinating construction. City announcements describe a building of at least 750,000 square feet, funded by a voter-approved one-cent sales tax plus MAPS 4 money and scheduled for completion in 2028. A venue that size typically depends on long-span steel for its roof and on welded connections, embeds and miscellaneous metals throughout, inspected to AWS D1.1 under the project specifications. Hotels, medical buildings, warehouses and school projects across the metro keep the same structural trades busy at a smaller scale.

Highways and bridges

I-35, I-40 and I-44 all pass through the Oklahoma City area, and the Oklahoma Department of Transportation keeps a steady program of bridge replacement and widening. Shop fabrication of steel girders falls under AWS D1.5, the bridge welding code, which carries a fracture control plan for nonredundant members, and field repairs and attachments bring the same code onto the job site.

Utilities and generation

OG&E, the electric utility headquartered in Oklahoma City, and the gas distribution companies serving the metro run generating plants, substations and gas systems that need welders during construction and maintenance outages. Power piping follows ASME B31.1 with Section IX procedures, which is why the ASME Part C option suits plant welders and the inspectors who check them.

Who hires CWIs in the Oklahoma City area, and what they look for

  • Midstream and pipeline contractors. Gathering and transmission work runs to API 1104, and spreads need inspectors who monitor welder qualification, preheat, fit-up and visual acceptance before the NDT crew arrives.
  • Oilfield fabrication shops. Shops building skids, production equipment, separators and compressor packages want QC staff who can check welds against procedures their customers have approved.
  • Operators' construction groups. Producers and midstream companies hire or contract inspectors to oversee stations, plants and tie-ins built by others.
  • Structural steel fabricators and erectors. The arena and the commercial and industrial pipeline of projects need D1.1 inspection in the shop and in the field, often alongside the special inspection the building code requires.
  • Aerospace contractors and suppliers. Companies supporting Tinker programs and other aviation customers value inspectors who are comfortable with tight aerospace specifications.
  • Third-party inspection firms. Owner's inspection and vendor surveillance across the state are common routes for CWIs who like variety; see inspection services in Oklahoma.

Job adverts in this market often name a code as well as the credential. "CWI with API 1104 experience" and "CWI, D1.1 structural" describe different jobs, and the Part C book you choose is part of how you answer them.

Which Part C code fits Oklahoma City work?

Part C is an open-book test on a code you pick when you apply. AWS offers AWS D1.1 for structural steel, API 1104 for pipelines, D1.2 for aluminum, D1.5 for bridges, D15.1 for railcars and locomotives, D17.1 for aerospace fusion welding, a combined ASME option covering Section IX with B31.1 and B31.3, and an ISO option. In central Oklahoma a handful of them cover almost everyone.

Study the edition named on your application and in the AWS exam reference material; it can be older than the copy on your shop's shelf. Background reading: API 1104, API 1104 acceptance criteria, AWS D1.1 and AWS D1.5.

The AWS Oklahoma City Section

Oklahoma City has its own AWS section, part of District 17 and separate from the Tulsa Section to the northeast. Its recent calendar shows what a section offers a CWI candidate: a welding contest run by Lampton Welding Supply at Wille Post Park in May 2026 that drew welders from Oklahoma and Kansas, and a technical meeting on stainless steel passivation, with a live demonstration, set for November 2026. Section meetings are where you meet working inspectors, QC managers and supervisors, and some of those people can verify the welding experience you list on the AWS application. The section's page, reachable through aws.org, carries the current schedule.

Where Oklahoma City welders learn the trade

Oklahoma's CareerTech network of technology centers is a large part of the local welding pipeline. Francis Tuttle Technology Center and Metro Technology Centers both run welding programs in Oklahoma City, and other technology center districts train welders around the state. Pipe welders also come up through union apprenticeships and through years on pipeline spreads and in oilfield shops, which is where many future inspectors first watch a CWI at work.

That schooling helps with the CWI in two ways. AWS counts completed trade or vocational courses toward eligibility, which lowers the experience requirement from the five years tied to a high school diploma to four, provided AWS accepts the courses. And a school transcript, an apprenticeship record or a file of welder qualification tests makes your history easier to document when AWS asks for verification.

Booking each part of the exam from Oklahoma City

When AWS accepts your application, it sends a confirmation carrying an eligibility code. You use that code to reserve the two computer-based parts, Fundamentals and Code Application, with Prometric; AWS says Prometric runs more than 100 test centers in the United States, so check its site for the one nearest you. Part B works differently. AWS runs the practical itself at its seminar and examination locations on dates it sets, so an Oklahoma candidate may have to travel out of state. Look at the current AWS seminar and examination schedule before you settle on a plan.

On the day, Part A is 150 questions. Part B combines hands-on tasks with tools and specimens AWS supplies and 46 written questions. Part C gives you roughly 50 to 65 questions with your code book open. AWS needs a score of at least 72 percent on each part and sends one consolidated report. AWS publishes its examination fees on aws.org, and Atlantis quotes the course separately on request. To budget the whole effort, including travel to a practical session, see the CWI exam budget planner; for what is known about difficulty by part, read CWI results by exam part.

Studying around rotations, well schedules and depot shifts

Oklahoma energy work does not keep office hours. Field hands on rotation have long stretches away and long stretches at home, station and plant crews see bursts of overtime around tie-ins and outages, and depot technicians work shifts. The online format was designed for that. One workable pattern: cover the fundamentals during a stretch at home, keep your code book in the truck and look up the clauses that govern the welds in front of you, practise Part B measurements on cut-outs and test coupons with your own gauges, and keep the timed papers for the run-up to your Prometric appointment. Questions can go to the instructor whenever they come up, day or night.

Corporate delivery: six days at an Oklahoma City-area employer

For a pipeline contractor, fabrication shop or structural steel company with several people to prepare, the six days can come to the company's own facility. Three things make that worthwhile. The practical work uses the company's gauges and welds, including production welds, cut-outs and welder test plates. The code day can split, so pipeline people work in API 1104 while shop QC staff work in D1.1 or the ASME book. And the dates can be fitted around field schedules, so nobody is pulled off a tie-in or a critical lift. Each candidate still applies to AWS personally and meets the eligibility and vision rules as an individual; no employer can submit those on someone else's behalf.

One-to-one preparation, online or in person

The one-to-one format gives one candidate six days of sessions with the instructor. They can run online, which works from a field camp with a reasonable connection, or in person at a location agreed when you book. The outline stays the same, but the time goes where that person needs it: symbols and fabrication math for someone strong on the shop floor, code navigation for an experienced welder who has never worked from a code book, or measurement drills for someone who has already cleared Parts A and C. Employers sometimes choose it for a single new QC lead who has to be ready before a contract starts.

Eligibility and the vision record for Oklahoma candidates

AWS ties the experience it requires to your education. A high school diploma or approved equivalent means five years of welding-related work; a bachelor's degree in welding engineering or welding technology means one; associate degrees, technical coursework and trade courses fall between, and less schooling means more years. The experience has to be verifiable and connected to welded products. AWS also needs a Visual Acuity Record on its form: near vision of Jaeger J2 at 12 inches or more, with or without glasses, plus a color perception test, done by a qualified practitioner and recent enough for AWS when you sit the exam. The full education table is on the AWS CWI course page, and the CWI requirements and career guide explains the rules in more depth. If you are short of the years, the AWS Certified Associate Welding Inspector (CAWI) has lower thresholds, though a CAWI works under a CWI or Senior CWI who makes final acceptance.

After the CWI: where Oklahoma City inspectors go next

AWS keeps the CWI valid for nine years, with renewal filings at the third and sixth years and recertification at the ninth. In this market inspectors tend to branch three ways. Pipeline inspectors build deep API 1104 experience and can add AWS code endorsements. Plant and station inspectors move toward the ASME side and owner's inspection roles. And many add nondestructive testing so they can perform ultrasonic, magnetic particle or penetrant tests themselves instead of waiting for a technician. That route runs through an employer's written practice under ASNT SNT-TC-1A, where the company certifies its own NDT technicians after training and documented method experience. Atlantis provides that training; see NDT training in Oklahoma City, VT Level 2 training and UT Level 2 training, and for the inspection side, weld inspection services. Inspectors who come to run programs can aim for the AWS Senior CWI; see the Senior CWI pathway. Atlantis offers API 510, 570 and 653 exam prep as separate self-paced online courses. Oklahoma inspectors deciding between credentials can read the CWI, API 577 and ASNT Level II comparison.

Nearby CWI pages and an Oklahoma City quote

Candidates elsewhere in the region can read the CWI exam prep pages for Tulsa, Wichita, Dallas and Fort Worth. To rehearse inspection steps in a browser, try Practical NDT for Oklahoma City or the welding workshop simulator.

For a quote, tell us which format you want (corporate, online or one-to-one), how many people are involved, each person's schooling and welding background in outline, and the Part C book each intends to choose. For delivery at your site, add the location, the gauges and sample welds available, and the weeks that avoid field commitments. Use the Oklahoma City CWI enquiry form.

faq.q: Is there an Atlantis CWI classroom in Oklahoma City?
faq.a: No. There is no Atlantis classroom in Oklahoma City. The six-day course reaches Oklahoma candidates three ways: corporate delivery at an employer's facility, online study at your own pace with an instructor answering questions, or six days of one-to-one sessions online or in person at a location agreed when booking. See the course outline.

The American Welding Society. AWS administers all three parts of the examination, decides who is eligible and issues the certification. The Atlantis course prepares Oklahoma candidates for that exam; it certifies no one, and it carries no AWS approval or endorsement.

faq.q: Which Part C code should a gathering-line or pipeline inspector in Oklahoma choose?
faq.a: API 1104. Federal pipeline safety rules incorporate it for pipeline welding, and it is the code those spreads and station tie-ins are built to. See API 1104.

faq.q: I work for a contractor supporting Tinker Air Force Base. Is D17.1 the right book?
faq.a: If your welding is aerospace hardware, AWS D17.1 is the Part C option closest to it. Depot repairs themselves follow Air Force technical orders, so check what your employer and contract actually reference before you choose.

faq.q: Where do Oklahoma City candidates take the CWI exam?
faq.a: Parts A and C are computer-based tests you book with Prometric using the eligibility code AWS sends. Part B, the practical, is run by AWS at its own seminar and examination locations on dates it sets, so you may need to travel out of state.

faq.q: Can I do the one-to-one sessions in person in Oklahoma City?
faq.a: In person is possible at a location agreed when you book, or the six days of one-to-one sessions can run online. Either way they follow the six-day outline and focus on the parts you find hardest.

faq.q: Can an oilfield fabrication shop have the six days delivered at its yard?
faq.a: Yes. Corporate delivery brings the six days to your facility and uses your gauges, production welds and welder test plates, with the code day split between API 1104, D1.1 or the ASME book as your group needs. Ask for a quote.

faq.q: Are the practice questions taken from AWS exams?
faq.a: No. Every practice question and timed paper is original, written by Atlantis against the subject areas AWS publishes. Atlantis has no access to the live examination.

faq.q: Does a CareerTech welding program count toward CWI eligibility?
faq.a: It can. AWS lists completed trade or vocational courses as reducing the experience requirement to four years, against five with a high school diploma, but AWS decides whether your courses qualify. Keep transcripts and welder test records with your application.

faq.q: How much does the course cost?
faq.a: Atlantis does not publish course prices; a quote is given on request for your format and group size. AWS publishes its own examination fees on aws.org, and the CWI exam budget planner lists the costs to plan for.
